title: Moving Mass Problem—Analytical Approximation of Transient Solution on Infinite Two-Layer Model
content: The problem of moving inertial objects traversing simplified models of railway tracks has an analytical solution in the transformed domain under the assumptions of linearity and longitudinal homogeneity of the model. However, the time-domain response usually requires numerical integration, which can be time-consuming and prone to numerical errors. Numerical integration could only be avoided if the inverse Laplace transform, i.e., the Bromwich integral, could be evaluated by contour integration as a sum of residues. This would only be possible if the poles of the function to be integrated were known and the function were continuous and vanished along the outer contour. There are, however, step discontinuities in the equivalent flexibility of these models, and therefore the sum of residues can only provide an approximation of the full solution. The full solution is composed of the steady-state part, corresponding to the moving force, and the unsteady harmonic motion attributed to the moving mass, which forms the main part of the transient response. There is also an additional term accounting for the aforementioned discontinuities. If this term is omitted, some differences can usually be observed within a small region near the initial instant, as the harmonic part is unable to match the initial conditions accurately without additional components. Nevertheless, this harmonic part identifies the dominant frequency of the transient solution, which is important for further analyses. Unfortunately, there are many cases in which the step discontinuities prevent the existence of the poles, the poles obtained are not related to the dominant frequency, or the associated vibration pattern is not correct. This contribution presents a way of dealing with such situations. A new technique for the determination of dominant frequencies is proposed and validated. It is shown how to estimate deflections with acceptable accuracy not only at the contact point, but also along the structure without numerical integration. It is also established how and why some existing poles should be disregarded. The new technique is basically analytical; the only numerical step consists of calculating the roots of a leading polynomial repeatedly. This new technique provides an approximation in the same sense as in the author’s previous works and therefore has the same advantages and limitations. The new feature is that dominant frequencies can be found in cases where the previous approach fails and that the agreement of deflections along the spatial coordinate is improved. The technique is new and, to the author’s knowledge, has not been previously published. Additionally, it is explained why the final response in undamped cases can resemble that of damped systems.
